notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Romans 16. Each point is followed by its source page.

**Gaps:** I found nothing on these sites from Orthodox sources (oca.org), from catholic.com or newadvent.org, or from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. My searches didn't turn up specifically Pentecostal or Lutheran treatments of the debated verses either. The only exceptions are Guzik (enduringword), Sam Storms, and Luther as quoted by Ligonier. My notes on vv. 8–15 and 21–23 are thin, and v. 26 is covered only as part of the closing doxology.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading.** Phoebe was on her way to Rome, probably carrying the letter, and Paul writes ahead so the church will welcome her. Her name comes from a title of Apollo, which suggests converts didn't feel they had to change pagan-sounding names. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
- **Ellicott:** "servant" should rather [be], a deaconess, keeping the technical term, and this is the first mention of women-deacons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/16-1.htm
- **Gill:** Phoebe was a deacon, not that she was a teacher of the word, or preacher of the Gospel. He also thinks she was more likely a wealthy woman serving out of her own money than a formally appointed deaconess. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/16-1.htm
- **The traditions disagree on whether this was an office:**
  - *Wesleyan:* Wesley says plainly that the Greek word is a deaconness. Clarke describes deaconesses as attending women at baptism, teaching people preparing for baptism, and visiting the sick and imprisoned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/16-1.html
  - *Reformed (TGC):* even conservative complementarian scholars believe that in this case, it refers to a female who was serving in some sort of official church office. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/can-women-be-deacons/ Another TGC writer says Romans 16 is precisely what an authentic complementarian should expect to find, with deacons distinct from elders. https://au.thegospelcoalition.org/article/men-and-women-in-romans-16-a-portrait-for-today/
  - *Charismatic (Sam Storms, a complementarian):* he thinks it likely Phoebe was a "deacon" of her church. He notes that evangelicals still argue over whether women may hold that office, though they agree the eldership is for men. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/women-in-the-life-of-the-church-romans-161-5a
  - *Against an office:* Coffman (Churches of Christ) denies that Paul's letters show any order of female deacons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/16-1.html GotQuestions says it is unclear whether she was a deacon or simply a servant. https://www.gotquestions.org/women-deacons.html
- **Catholic view:** Haydock describes her as one of the women in ministry who privately taught catechumens, helped at the baptism of women and handed out charity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/16-1.html

**v. 2**
- The word translated "help" (prostatis) properly signifies a patron, which suggests she had wealth and influence (Benson). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/16-1.htm
- **Utley:** the word originally meant a wealthy patroness. Letters of recommendation like this one were meant to secure material support for travelling ministers. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0
- **Matthew Henry:** Paul is asking for help for someone who has herself helped many. he that watereth shall be watered also himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm

**v. 3**
- **Utley:** Prisca is often named before her husband, which was unusual in that culture. She may have been of Roman nobility or the stronger personality of the two. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0
- **Guzik**, quoting Spurgeon: this couple is the opposite of Ananias and Sapphira, a husband and wife united in sincere devotion rather than in hypocrisy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 4**
- **Utley:** "risked their necks" is an idiom from the executioner's axe, and Scripture doesn't say what event Paul means. The thanks of "all the churches of the Gentiles" may refer to their help to Apollos (Acts 18). https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0

**v. 5**
- **House church:** the church met in homes, and there were no church buildings until the third century. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0 Guzik adds that a city would have several house congregations, each probably with its own "pastor." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
- **Epenetus:** Utley takes "Asia" to mean the Roman province in western Turkey. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0 Guzik follows the NKJV reading "Achaia." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 6**
- **Utley:** nothing is known about Mary. She may have been a missionary from the Roman church. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0

**v. 7 — the most debated verse**
- **Man or woman?** Only the accent mark separates Junias (male) from Junia (female). The female name is common in Latin, while the male form is almost unknown, with only one ancient instance (NET notes). https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Rom&chapter=16&verse=7 Utley adds that "Junias" has never been found in Roman inscriptions. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0
- **"Among" or "to" the apostles?** The NET Bible follows Burer and Wallace in reading "well known *to* the apostles." It adds that if Junia was a woman, she may have had the gift of apostleship rather than the office. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Rom&chapter=16&verse=7 GotQuestions agrees: It is unlikely that Junia was an apostle. It also notes that Chrysostom counted her among the apostles. https://www.gotquestions.org/Junia-Junias-apostle.html A TGC writer says The grammar works both ways. https://au.thegospelcoalition.org/article/men-and-women-in-romans-16-a-portrait-for-today/
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel):** the phrase suggests they were apostles in the wider sense of special messengers, not members of the Twelve. This is the strongest evidence for women apostles, but "it isn't very strong." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
- **Utley:** the context suggests the wider sense of "apostle," but the definite article points to the Twelve. He urges caution about being dogmatic on women in ministry. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0
- **Early church:** Origen calls Junia a woman "worthy of the appellation of apostle." https://biblehub.com/q/Is_Junia_a_female_apostle_in_Romans_16_7.htm
- **"In Christ before me":** Henry notes how readily Paul gave others precedence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm

**v. 8**
- A tomb in Rome's earliest Christian catacomb, from the late first or early second century, bears the name AMPLIAS. Some link it to this man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 9**
- **Henry:** Paul's warm words ("beloved") show that Where the law of love is in the heart the law of kindness will be in the tongue. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm

**v. 10**
- Paul greets the household of Aristobulus but not the man himself. Spurgeon took this to mean Aristobulus was unconverted while his household believed, and preached on that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
- **Utley:** Aristobulus and Herodion may be names from Jewish noble families. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0

**v. 11**
- Henry counts Herodion among Paul's relatives. He says faith doesn't remove our respect for family but sanctifies it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm

**v. 12**
- **Spurgeon (via Guzik):** Persis "labored much," while others simply "labored." Honour among believers is graded by service done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 13**
- This Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21), but the name was common. Guzik says "chosen" means eminent, not elect. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/ (Other Reformed readers might take "chosen" differently, but I didn't find their comments on this verse.)

**vv. 14–15**
- Thirteen of the 24 names appear in inscriptions linked to the emperor's palace, so Paul may be greeting believers in Caesar's household (Phil 4:22). Guzik also suggests Nereus may be the servant of a Roman couple condemned as Christians in AD 95. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
- **Henry:** Paul ends with "all the saints" so that no one feels forgotten. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm

**v. 16**
- The kiss was an ordinary greeting at the time (Luke 7:45). Clement of Alexandria later complained the practice was being abused. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 17**
- **Guzik:** the verse covers both dividers and deceivers. "Truth without unity leads to pride; unity without truth leads to a departure from the true gospel." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
- **Henry:** some think Paul especially means the Judaizing teachers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm

**v. 18**
- **Henry:** like the serpent with Eve, these teachers corrupt people's judgment by first winning their affections. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm
- **Guzik:** such people usually see themselves as noble crusaders, but their motives are selfish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 19**
- **Guzik:** knowing the genuine is a better defence than studying the counterfeit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
- **Henry:** Paul praises the Romans first so the warning lands gently, and a famous church's errors spread widely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_016.cfm

**v. 20**
- **Genesis 3:15:** Generations of Christian interpreters have found in today's passage an allusion to Genesis 3:15. Luther took "Satan" to include "the devil, and whoever follows him." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/satan-crushed-under-our-feet
- **When is "soon"? The commentators differ on timing:**
  - *Calvin:* the verse is a promise, not a prayer. It isn't only about the last day; God would soon subdue Satan, who was raging at the time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/16-20.html
  - *Piper (Baptist):* he reads it mainly as the final crushing of Satan (Rev 20), with "your feet" because Christ's victory is ours. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-god-of-peace-will-soon-crush-satan-under-your-feet
  - *Ellicott:* Paul probably expected the Messiah to return soon. https://biblehub.com/romans/16-20.htm
  - *Haldane:* the verse is about a present victory. https://biblehub.com/sermons/romans/16-20.htm
- **Maclaren:** God does the bruising, but He uses our feet to do it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/16-20.htm

**v. 21**
- Timothy is named first as Paul's closest associate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 22**
- Tertius wrote the letter down as Paul dictated. This is the only letter where Paul's secretary is named. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 23**
- Gaius was so well known for hospitality that he hosted "the whole church." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/

**v. 24 (textual question)**
- The verse is missing from the older manuscripts and from the Vulgate. Utley says it is obviously not original with Paul. https://bible.org/seriespage/romans-16-0
- **Ellicott:** the blessing belongs at v. 20, not at v. 24. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/15.htm
- **Gamble (modern scholar), as reported by NET:** he argues for keeping v. 24 and placing the doxology after 14:23. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rom+16%3A25-27

**vv. 25–27**
- **Placement:** manuscripts put the doxology after 14:23, after 15:33, or after 16:23. NET concludes it almost certainly belongs in Romans; it is only a question of where, and judges that the evidence favours its place after 16:23. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rom+16%3A25-27
- **Meaning:**
  - *Guzik:* Paul entrusts the Romans to "Him who is able to establish you." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-16/
  - *Benson:* Paul gives thanks for the calling of the Gentiles, foretold in the prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/16-24.html
  - *Utley:* the doxology sums up the letter's main themes, possibly in Paul's own handwriting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/romans-16.html
  - *Bullinger (dispensational):* he thinks Paul added the doxology later, from prison in Rome. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/romans-16.html
